routes.speaker: Dustin Crummett

bridges.statement: Subjects of experience are simple, indivisible, nonphysical souls rather than material objects.
Hemisphere-transplant cases reveal determinate facts of personal identity that do not supervene on physical facts.
Mind–brain correlations are governed by contingent psychophysical laws rather than necessary supervenience.
Soul–body interaction may be a basic causal relation and need not operate through a further mechanism.
Conceivable variations in consciousness and identity provide evidence against necessary physical dependence.

routes.position: The soul exists as a nonphysical aspect of persons

routes.speaker: Ben Watkins

bridges.statement: The evidence does not support the existence of a nonphysical soul.
Mental changes have sufficient physical causes and mental properties necessarily depend on physical properties.
Dual-aspect monism preserves irreducible mentality without positing a distinct mental substance.
Causal closure and conservation of energy count against causal interaction with a nonphysical realm.
Personal identity is reducible to psychological connectedness rather than an enduring soul.
Neuroscience, genetics, and comparative brain morphology favor physical dependence over independent souls.

routes.position: The case for a nonphysical soul is unsuccessful

sections.title: The Mind–Body Framework and Rival Ontologies
sections.rationale: Establishes the shared anti-reductionist starting points and the competing substance-dualist and dual-aspect-monist explanations.

sections.title: Transplants, Subjects, and Personal Identity
sections.rationale: Contains Crummett's principal positive argument and Watkins's reductionist response concerning what survives hemisphere division and transplantation.

sections.title: Mental Causation and Physical Closure
sections.rationale: Addresses whether nonphysical causation is intelligible and compatible with conservation of energy.

sections.title: Supervenience, Necessity, and Conceivability
sections.rationale: Tests whether observed mind–brain regularities establish necessary dependence and whether conceivable counterexamples undermine it.

sections.title: Comparative Explanatory Power
sections.rationale: Compares contingent psychophysical laws with necessary dependence using brain damage, genetics, animals, and theoretical simplicity.

selectionBalanceAudit.rationale: The transplant section is necessarily asymmetric because Crummett's opening case contains four separately load-bearing inferences: the fission trilemma, the rejection of partial identity, the claim that experiential identity is determinate rather than conventional, and the extrinsic-identity objection. Watkins answers those related claims together through one unified Parfit-style no-self and psychological-connectedness response; splitting that response would duplicate a single inference.
